label: paragraph_title
text: “UNEQUAL” TREATIES!

label: text
text: It does not greatly matter to the Powers what kind of Government or Governments are installed in China, save and except any that are determined to flout international Treaties and menace the lives, and property of foreigners. In the latter case it is, and always will be, the bounden duty of the respective Powers to take all adequate measures to bring such a Government to their senses, and to teach them that Treaties are made to be respected by both contracting parties thereto. If any particular Treaty or Treaties are regarded by any section of the Chinese to be "unequal" or unfair the blame therefore cannot wholly be laid on the shoulders of the Powers; equally culpable must be those Chinese statesmen who put their signatures thereto. To condemn certain Treaties as "unequal" is merely to castigate China herself. Why should the "foreign Imperialists" — that catchword of the pro-Bolshevist party in China—alone have to bear all the brunt and be singled out for venomous attacks? Those Chinese who indulge in such claptraps as "hunting dogs of the foreigners," the "foreign Imperialists," and so forth are atrociously poor students of China's own past history. Treaties are made for a purpose. They are framed in accordance with the exigencies of the moment. If certain of the terms are harsh, that in itself implies a previous falling from grace of one of the contracting parties. But Treaties can always be reviewed. They can be abrogated, repealed, amended, or modified at some later date. Under altered circumstances no civilised nation would stand for the continuance of Treaties the terms of which are obsolete and, therefor, "unequal" by the virtue of altered circumstances. Moreover, what does

label: text
text: the League of Nations exist for if it is not to examine such grievances as “unequal” Treaties?

label: text
text: In the scrapping of old Treaties and the framing of new Treaties, however, regard must be had to the prevailing mentality of both contracting parties and the will and the ability of both to ensure the due fulfilment of all obligations undertaken. If it takes two to make a quarrel it likewise takes two to keep a Treaty. Is China to-day in a fit state to be given new Treaties—Treaties, that is of a nature that she could regard as an improvement on the old? The whole country is disrupted by civil war. There is no strong Central Government. The North and South are at daggers drawn, each endeavouring by hook or by crook to gain the ultimate permanent mastery. And yet, in the height of all this welter of blood and amid all the "buying" of Generals by the opposing factions, certain sections in China can find time to repeat the parrot cries of "unequal Treaties," "the yoke of the foreigners," "the hunting dogs of the foreigners," etc., and to pour out on the Powers volleys of verbal abuse! That, surely, is a very ill-advised way in which to plead for the abolition of "unequal" Treaties!, The violation of existing Treaties, at the bidding of the emissaries of Moscow, surely cannot strike the most sagacious of China's leaders as an ideal method of securing relief from "unequal" Treaties. The threat of not abstaining from the illegal boycott of foreign goods for a single day is not likely to impress outsiders with the sincerity of China's case in her relations with the Powers! If "unequal" Treaties do exist, it looks as if the greatest cause for grievance lies on the side of the Powers by the continuous and provocative breaches thereof by the Chinese.

label: paragraph_title
text: Viva a Republica Portugueza.

label: text
text:
Sixteen years ago to-day a republic was proclaimed in Portugal and a provisional Government was established with Dr. Théophile Braga as the Provisional President. To-day the Portuguese community of Hong Kong are celebrating the birthday of their Republic, and on behalf of our readers, we extend to them hearty and cordial greetings. The reasons for which Portugal is neglected are precisely those which in some eyes make her lovable. For half a century art has done almost nothing for the natural river highways: and the Douro, the Guadiana and the Tagus flow through the country like wandering rivulets of great English parks. The large towns of the interior look like pretty kiosks; rising above flowing thickets: peaceful retreats, solitude animated with a life that jogs along quietly and does not go with leaps and bounds as in France, where a satisfied humanity stands still, instead of rushing into the unknown risks of the future. Truly a child-like nature, satisfied with little, pursuing the ideal, economical without avarice, pure in morals, sober, generous, hospitable, the Portuguese have bred heroes in place of diplomats, poets in place of capitalists, they knew how bravely to defend their country against the Romans, the Arabs and the Spaniards, and still more recently, against the army of Napoleon. They have kept themselves a free nation, independent and original, possessing a language, a literature, distinct manners and customs, and governed politically since 1910, by one of the most liberal constitutions in Europe.
Viva a Republica Portuguese

label: paragraph_title
text: INTERPORT: LAWN BOWLS

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir,—As a player of the game of lawn bowls, I wish to take exception to uncharitable remarks published both by Mr. Wom. Wotherspoon (vice-president of the H.K.L.B.A., and skip of the Interport team against Shanghai) and by Mr. C. J. Tacchi (hon. sec. to the H.K.L.B.A. and a member of the selection committee).

label: text
text: In the interests of the game and if a public scandal is to be avoided, I wish to ask the controversialists to restrict themselves "to " facts. Mr. Wotherspoon has had his say, Mr. Tacchi has followed and you publish a denial of imagination.

label: text
text: Passages objected to as showing signs of bias outside of the issue are:—

label: paragraph_title
text: By Mr. Wotherspoon:—

label: text
text: "To me it still seems absurd that a man who had resigned from the Selection Committee and played for his place as a player and got badly beaten in the trial game should have been afterwards put on as the all powerful selector of the team."

label: text
text: I fail to see how a man's playing capacity has anything to do with this selection capabilities. If selectors must be players par excellence there would be no need to pick anybody else. One can be a rotten player but a fine judge.

label: text
text: "I would here emphasise that Mr. Gow, although putting himself forward as a candidate for playing in this. Interport team, had never during the past season played in any League matches."

label: text
text: All the emphasis Mr. Wotherspoon can lay will make no difference—obviously a red herring. The biggest mug can put himself forward as a candidate for Vice Chancellor of Cambridge (and may get the job). Mr. Gov's absence from the League has nothing to do with his captaincy, managership, or any other association with the H.K. interport combination. The H.K.L.B.A. gave him certain authority and they are the highest local authority for the game.

label: text
text: I agree with Mr. Wotherspoon when he says that "Mr. Gow's appointment as sole dictator was very unfortunate for Hong Kong." The chopping and changing could not have conducted to getting the best teamwork.

label: text
text: As, regard Mr. Wotherspoon's account of his part in the inter-port game," an impartial critic can only—on what he provides—exonerate him from failure and give him credit for having done his very best.

label: text
text: If Mr. Wotherspoon was satisfied with the selection committee he would not have proposed an amendment.

label: text
text: "The inference to be drawn from this is that he considers him to be the only bowler in Hong Kong capable of acting as Captain of the team," assuming, of course, that he has no personal animosity against Mr. Gow. He goes on to state that Mr. Holland and himself both understood that the team had been selected in Hong Kong. It would be interesting to know from what source this vital understanding was obtained."

label: text
text:
The first sentence is very uncharitable and falls altogether if it was meant to be a scathing criticism. Mr. Wotherspoon thought he was the skip and captain of the tour, the other matches being subsidiary to the interports.
Re the second and third sentences: Why did not Mr. Tacchi at the time publish the team as officially chosen?" And if the team published by you was wrong why did Mr. Tacchi not deny it?
The last two paragraphs are

label: text
text:
To you and all concerned, Sir, I would point out that everything in black and white is the best preventative. Mr. Wotherspoon erred in not asking for a mandate but took things for granted. The selection committee erred in not defining the position beforehand. Mr. Gow had his authority and acted on it, but unwisely in aiming at "the maximum of fun for everybody" instead of concentrating on one rink. Meanwhile I advise everybody including myself to shut up forthwith instead of washing linen.... ad intexim.
When the "Sunday Herald" has answered the obvious question Mr. Wotherspoon asks (on personal playing honours) the matter is completely closed.

label: text
text: H.K.-CANTON RELATIONS

label: text
text:
Sir, — Your correspondent, G. K. Chang, says in his letter in your issue to-day that the Canton Government is "our undesirable neighbour."
In my opinion, the contrary is the truth. Canton is our most desirable neighbour because Hong Kong has on numerous occasions expressed its friendship and goodwill towards Canton.
Everybody in this Colony, except of course G. K. Chang, wants to call off this boycott and to resume normal relation and traffic between us and that city.

label: text
text: These are the undeniable facts. If Canton is an "undesirable neighbour," why not let the present condition remain, where it is? We mind our own business, and Canton takes care of itself. But facts show that the continuation of "friendly terms between Hong Kong and Canton is desired by all save perhaps your correspondent, G. K. Chang.

label: text
text: Your correspondent is unduly alarmed in saying that with the resumption of intercourse between the two ports, there will be a tremendous amount of 'Red' element pouring out from Canton into this Island to conduct their mischievous service.

label: text
text:
Assuming for the sake of argument only, if there are "reds" wishing to start trouble here, they should come now. They can come here now with as much ease as after the "settlement of the boycott. Why wait?
What evidence has your correspondent in supporting such statement? No suggestion has been made to Canton asking that no Reds be permitted to come to Hong Kong. The truth is that Canton has no more Reds than New York or London.
The Hong Kong Government knows how to handle the situation, and your correspondent's Red advice serves no other purpose than to create ill-feeling which sensible persons like to avoid.

label: paragraph_title
text: USE OF WORD "KWAI"

label: text
text:
[To the Editor of the "China Mail."]:
Sir,—I read with interest the letter of "Refinement" published in your paper last Thursday on the subject of the use of "Kwai" among the illiterate class of the Chinese community. I am glad that "Refinement" finds that this now commons expression to denote all foreigners is only used among this class. From my own experience in many parts of China I have found this expression used by all classes and in the majority of cases without any idea of inflicting an insult but just as an expression to indicate the foreigner.

label: text
text: I think in a large number of cases the main trouble between Chinese and foreigners is that both sides are too apt to imagining insults where none is meant.

label: text
text:
[To the Editor of the "China Mail"]
Sir Y our correspondent
"Monitor" raises an interesting question and, synchronising as his letter did, with Captain Cobnam's return from his flight to Australia, provides material for much study.

label: text
text: In the course of this speech when introducing the air estimates in the House of Commons last February, Sir Samuel Hoare, Secretary of State for Air, said that his air policy was to provide Home defence against air attack: to provide air defence in suitable parts of the Empire to undertake the required air work for the Army and Navy: to develop civil air routes over the face of the Empire and to "help the British people to become a people of the air".

label: text
text:
Sir Samuel, Hoare is certainly to be congratulated upon his policy as regards the promotion of civil flying and the expansion of air knowledge. The growing safety and controllability of aeroplanes has an important bearing upon the newest and most significant of all developments in aviation—that of the popular State-aided flying club. There are, I understand, already five light aeroplane clubs in Britain with over a thousand members. A sum of £30,000 is being spent by the Air Ministry in the encouragement of this scheme and it may be anticipated that further grants will follow. That State aid is well justified may be judged from the fact that each pilot trained by the clubs will be expected to join the Royal Air Force Reserve, and this means that Britain will be building up that human reservoir of air power which will be all-important in any emergency of the future. In another great world struggle, should it come, aeroplanes of metal will pour from the factories upon a mass production plan and the great problem will not be machines, but airmen; hence the national importance of any movement which produces pilots in times of peace.
Yours, etc.
Hong Kong, October 5.

label: paragraph_title
text: SILVER WEDDING.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRESENTATION TO MR. GEOG. DUNCAN.

label: text
text: Yesterday a presentation was made to Mr. G. Duncan of the H. K. Whampon Dock Co. on the occasion of his silver wedding. A large number of the European members of the staff gathered in the Reading Room under the Chairmanship of Mr. Macaskill who said there may have been silver weddings among them before but this was a case where they had been married in the Dock. He hoped that though most of them did not expect to be there they would hear of their Golden Wedding. The presentation was made by Mr. R. Lapsley, the oldest member of the Dock Staff. He said he felt grateful to be allowed to make the presentation as his wife had been Mrs. Duncan's bridesmaid. Mr. Duncan, he continued, was a man who was always willing to go out of his way, to do extra work and to help others.

label: text
text:
Mr. Duncan suitably replied, saying that, on looking round he saw several who were there when he received his wedding present from the then staff. He told them they should not talk so much of him as of his wife as she had a great deal to do with everything. In his case the phrase "better half" did not express nearly enough.
Mr. Scott added:—
All of you are as well aware as I how excellent a man our friend Mr. Duncan is, and I venture to say to his face what all of us think that no more steadfast friend, no cheerer chum exists amongst us although we have many kind friends and neighbours in our midst.

label: text
text: Twenty-five years is a long spell gentleman, it exceeds one-third of the generally allotted span of our existence, for that space of time however our friends Mr. and Mrs. Duncan have been united by the most sacred ties by which, we mortals can be bound.

label: text
text:
All those years they have stood as an example of domestic felicity and we have watched with interest and affection the sons growing up to manhood, the ornaments of this truly domestic hearth.
So gentlemen, let us be merry, it is the twenty-fifth anniversary of a happy day, often to be overtaken let us hope in future years.
The spring is gone, it may be the summer is passing, perhaps; but there is yet the golden autumn of their lives to come when the harvest of good seeds shall be reaped in troops of friends and loving memories.
Tonsts were given with musical honours and several old friends of Mr. Duncan's said a few words after which an impromptu concert was held.
